journal_name: Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience

abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for understanding concurrency dynamics in heterogeneous many-core architectures, fundamentally reorienting how we model resource contention in modern parallel systems. Unlike conventional approaches that assume homogeneous processing elements, our model embraces architectural diversity by introducing a probabilistic concurrency tensor that captures asymmetric communication patterns and divergent execution velocities across heterogeneous cores. We formalize this paradigm through a set of axioms governing resource arbitration in systems where CPU, GPU, and specialized accelerators coexist. The theoretical analysis reveals that traditional scheduling algorithms operating under homogeneity assumptions incur up to 47% efficiency loss when deployed on heterogeneous substrates. Our framework enables precise prediction of throughput degradation under varying workload compositions, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to existing analytical models. Furthermore, we prove that optimal concurrency degrees are architecture-dependent and cannot be universal constants, establishing a new theoretical foundation for workload characterization in high-performance computing environments. This paradigm shift transforms how practitioners conceptualize parallel algorithm design for next-generation computing platforms, moving from one-size-fits-all approaches toward architecture-aware concurrency optimization.

We present an enhanced analytical model for predicting performance bottlenecks in distributed computing systems that significantly improves upon existing queueing theory approaches. Our contribution addresses the fundamental limitation of classical models that assume Markovian service times, which poorly represent real-world parallel workloads exhibiting heavy-tailed distributions and temporal correlations. The proposed framework integrates fractal renewal processes with traditional network calculus to capture long-range dependence inherent in big data applications. Through rigorous mathematical derivation, we establish closed-form expressions for response time distributions that account for both spatial contention across distributed nodes and temporal correlation within job streams. Experimental validation using traces from production cloud computing infrastructure demonstrates prediction accuracy improvements of 28-35% compared to baseline models across diverse workload categories including scientific computing simulations and data-intensive MapReduce jobs. Our analysis further provides actionable insights for capacity planning, revealing that modest increases in buffer sizes yield disproportionate performance gains when temporal correlation is explicitly managed. This work advances the theoretical foundations of performance analysis for distributed systems while providing practitioners with more reliable prediction tools for system optimization.

This paper introduces Hermes, a groundbreaking distributed runtime system designed for the era of disaggregated datacenter architectures. Hermes represents a fundamental departure from traditional co-located execution models by enabling fine-grained computation migration across physically separated CPU, memory, and accelerator pools connected via high-speed interconnects. Our system employs a novel concurrency-aware memory coherence protocol that maintains consistency without requiring physical data movement, instead using logical migration through capability-based addressing. The architecture supports diverse parallel programming models through a unified abstraction layer, allowing seamless execution of both message-passing and shared-memory applications on the same infrastructure. Performance evaluation conducted on a 512-node testbed demonstrates that Hermes achieves 3.2x throughput improvement for latency-sensitive workloads compared to state-of-the-art disaggregated systems while maintaining strict fault tolerance guarantees through lightweight checkpointing mechanisms. For GPU computing workloads, our design enables dynamic resource reallocation that reduces average job completion time by 41%. Hermes fundamentally reimagines how concurrency is managed in future computing substrates, establishing a new design paradigm for high-performance computing infrastructure that naturally accommodates the increasing heterogeneity and physical distribution of modern hardware.

We present an improved fault tolerance framework for large-scale scientific computing workflows that substantially advances the state-of-the-art in checkpoint-restart mechanisms. Our system, called Sentinel, addresses the critical challenge of maintaining job progress in high-performance computing environments where failures are becoming increasingly frequent as system scales expand. Sentinel introduces a hybrid checkpointing strategy that dynamically balances between application-level and system-level checkpoints based on real-time failure prediction derived from hardware telemetry analysis. The design incorporates intelligent checkpoint placement algorithms that minimize interference with concurrent applications while ensuring rapid recovery. Our implementation integrates seamlessly with existing parallel programming models including MPI and OpenMP, requiring minimal code modifications. Extensive evaluation across three production supercomputing facilities using representative scientific computing applications demonstrates that Sentinel reduces checkpoint overhead by 52% compared to conventional periodic checkpointing while improving overall workflow completion rates by 18%. For long-running big data analytics jobs, our system achieves near-optimal fault tolerance with only 3-7% resource overhead. This work provides the high-performance computing community with a practical solution for resilient execution that scales to exascale systems while maintaining efficiency.
